<!-- README.md -->

# autocomplete: fast tab completion for macOS bash 3.2

**Fast tab completion for the stock macOS bash 3.2 (`/bin/bash`), written in C.**

macOS still ships bash 3.2 from 2007, and most modern completion tools have dropped support
for it. This project was built specifically for that bash. All completion logic runs in a
single compiled C binary, so pressing TAB doesn't run any shell code. Completion is
instant and new terminals open as fast as before.

```console
$ docker run --network <TAB>
bridge   host   none   my_app_default
$ git checkout fe<TAB>
$ git checkout feature/login
$ make in<TAB>
$ make install
```

It is a lightweight alternative to bash-completion that completes docker, git, kubectl, make,
mvn, npm and more. You don't need Homebrew bash, the `bash-completion` package or zsh, and
there are no shell scripts. It shines on parameter monsters like curl and wget. Hundreds of
flags are grouped to fit your screen, and TAB on an empty argument shows ready-made usage
examples.

## Why another bash completion tool?

If you use bash on a Mac, you've probably found that completion tools don't support it:

- **bash-completion 2.x** requires bash 4.2 or newer.
- **bash-completion 1.3**, the last version that runs on bash 3.2, is unmaintained. It
  loads every completion script at shell startup, which makes each new terminal slow to open.
- The usual workaround is to `brew install bash` and change your login shell.

autocomplete works with the bash already on your Mac:

- **Built for macOS bash 3.2.** Tested against Apple's `/bin/bash` and Apple clang.
- **Fast because it's all C.** Bash registers the binary with `complete -C`, so every TAB
  calls the binary directly. No bash functions, no `sed`/`awk` pipelines, no subshells.
- **Fast shell startup.** The init line registers commands and loads nothing else. Specs
  are read only when you press TAB.
- **No dependencies.** One binary, plain C, builds with the Xcode Command Line Tools.

## Features

- Bundled completions for **docker**, **git**, **kubectl**, **make**, **mvn**, **java**,
  **python**, **node**, **npx**, **bun**, **bunx**, **npm**, **yarn**, **pnpm**, **pip**, **go**,
  **cargo**, **gradle**, **brew**, **gh**, **ssh**, **scp**, **terraform**, **helm**, **aws**,
  **tmux**, **kill**, **pkill**, **killall**, **jq**, **curl**, **wget**, **code** (VS Code),
  macOS **open**, **launchctl**, **defaults**, **diskutil**, **say**, **caffeinate**, **pbcopy**,
  **pbpaste**, **sips**, **screencapture**, and `autocomplete` itself.
- Wrapper commands **sudo**, **env**, **time**, **xargs** complete the command after them with
  that command's own completion (`sudo git chec<TAB>` → `checkout`).
- Live values from your environment:
  - docker: running containers, images, networks, volumes
  - git: branches, tags, remotes, stashes, changed files
  - kubectl: namespaces, contexts, pods, nodes, resource types
  - npm: `package.json` scripts and dependencies
  - mvn: profiles and modules from `pom.xml`, plugin goals for plugins the project uses
  - make: Makefile targets and variables, with descriptions from `## text` or the comment
    above each target (honors `make -C dir` and `make -f file`)
  - killall, pkill: your running process names; kill, `caffeinate -w`: PIDs with process names
  - say: voices with language and sample text (`say -v Ed<TAB>`), audio devices
  - code: installed extensions for `--uninstall-extension`/`--disable-extension`
  - sips: property keys with types for `-g`/`-s`; screencapture: app bundle ids for `-B`
  - ssh, scp: hosts from `~/.ssh/config` and `known_hosts` (`scp gr<TAB>` → `grafana:`)
  - brew: installed formulae and services
  - gh: pull requests, issues, workflow runs, gists, labels, releases, repos
  - yarn, pnpm: `package.json` scripts, dependencies and workspace packages
  - pip: installed packages; go: packages and test names; cargo: bins, examples, tests
  - terraform: resources from state, `*.tfvars`; helm: releases, repo charts, namespaces
  - node: `package.json` scripts for `--run`, test reporters; npx, bunx: binaries in `node_modules/.bin`
  - bun: scripts, dependencies (`remove`, `why`, `update`), `node_modules/.bin` for `bun x`
  - python: module names for `-m` (`python3 -m http<TAB>` → `http.server`)
  - java: module names (`-m`, `--add-modules`), jars and class paths
  - aws: profiles, regions, S3 buckets; tmux: sessions and buffers
  - open: app names (`-a`) and bundle ids (`-b`); launchctl: services and LaunchAgent plists
- Descriptions next to subcommands and flags when several match
  (`git stash <TAB>` → `pop  -- Apply a stash and remove it`).
- Usage examples for commands with hundreds of flags: `curl <TAB>` and `wget <TAB>` list
  common recipes (`📌 -X  -- curl -X DELETE https://httpbin.org/delete   📚 any other
  method: PUT, PATCH, DELETE`) instead of nothing.
- Handles `--flag=value`, `image:tag`, quoted words and file names with spaces.
- Add a command by writing a small YAML file, with no rebuild
  ([how](docs/adding-commands.md)).
- Generate flag completion for system commands like `ps`, `ls` or `tar` from their man
  pages ([details](docs/man-pages.md)).
- Complete shell aliases like the command they wrap (`autocomplete alias kubectl k`).
- Very large specs (over 100 KB) are compiled to a cache, so TAB doesn't re-parse YAML.

## Requirements

- macOS with the Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`) for `cc` and `make`.
- bash 3.2 (the macOS `/bin/bash`) or any newer bash.

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/hza/bash-autocomplete.git autocomplete
cd autocomplete
make install
```

`make install`:

- installs the binary to `/usr/local/bin/autocomplete`,
- installs the bundled specs to `/usr/local/share/autocomplete/`,
- precompiles any spec over 100 KB into the cache,
- adds `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` to `~/.bashrc`, unless it's already there.

Open a new terminal (or run `source ~/.bashrc`) and press TAB after `docker`, `git` or `make`.

> macOS Terminal starts login shells, which read `~/.bash_profile`, not `~/.bashrc`.
> `make install` warns if your `~/.bash_profile` doesn't load `~/.bashrc`; add
> `[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc` to it.

Options:

```sh
make install PREFIX=$HOME/.local          # install without sudo (put ~/.local/bin on PATH first)
make install PROFILE=$HOME/.bash_profile  # use a different startup file
```

If `/usr/local` isn't writable, use `sudo make install`. In that case the cache isn't built
during install; it's built on your first completion instead.

### Using it without installing

```sh
make
eval "$(./autocomplete bash)"                     # recommended
source /dev/stdin <<<"$(./autocomplete bash)"     # if you prefer `source`
```

> `source <(autocomplete bash)` does **not** work in bash 3.2. A long-standing bash bug
> makes it silently read nothing. Use one of the forms above.

### Uninstalling

```sh
make uninstall          # use the same PREFIX / PROFILE you installed with
```

This removes the binary, the bundled specs, their cache files and the exact `eval` line
from your profile. Your own specs in `~/.config/autocomplete` are left untouched.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `autocomplete bash` | Print the bash init script (use with `eval`). |
| `autocomplete list` | List commands that have a spec. |
| `autocomplete check FILE` | Validate a spec and print how it was understood (as JSON). |
| `autocomplete cache [NAME...]` | Precompile specs over 100 KB into the cache (all if no names). |
| `autocomplete from man [--force] CMD...` | Write `~/.config/autocomplete/CMD.yaml` from `man CMD`. |
| `autocomplete alias [--force] CMD NAME...` | Complete `NAME` (e.g. a shell alias) like `CMD` by symlinking `~/.config/autocomplete/NAME.yaml` to its spec. |
| `autocomplete alias --rm NAME...` | Remove aliases made by `autocomplete alias` (only symlinks are removed). |
| `autocomplete alias --list` | List aliases as `NAME -> CMD`. |

## FAQ

### How do I get tab completion for git and docker in macOS bash?

Install autocomplete (`make install`) and open a new terminal. You don't need Homebrew
bash, `bash-completion` or zsh.

### Do I need to upgrade bash or switch to zsh?

No. autocomplete is designed for the bash 3.2 that macOS ships as `/bin/bash`.

### Why is it faster than bash-completion?

bash-completion is written in bash and sources its scripts into every shell.
autocomplete keeps all logic in a compiled C binary that runs only when you press TAB.
Shell startup does nothing beyond one `complete` registration.

### Can I add completion for my own command?

Yes. Write `~/.config/autocomplete/<command>.yaml` describing subcommands, flags and
values. See [Adding your own commands](docs/adding-commands.md).

## Building from source

```sh
make            # builds ./autocomplete
make clean
```

The code is plain C with no dependencies: `autocomplete.c` (engine), `yaml.c` (YAML
reader and writer) and `manparse.c` (man page reader). Bundled specs live in `specs/`.

<!-- docs/adding-commands.md -->

# Adding your own commands

Drop a YAML file into `~/.config/autocomplete/`, named after the command:

```yaml
# ~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml
flags:
  --context: {value: any, description: Name of the kubeconfig context}
commands:
  logs:
    description: Print the logs of a pod    # shown when several commands match
    flags:
      -f: {description: Stream the logs}    # no "value": the flag takes none
    args:
      exec: kubectl get pods -o name | cut -d/ -f2
  apply:
    flags:
      -f: {value: file, description: File to apply}
```

Then run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again (or open a new terminal).

Check the file for mistakes with:

```sh
autocomplete check ~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml
```

Later edits to the file take effect on the next TAB; only adding a *new* command needs the
`eval` step.

## Shell aliases

If you have `alias dk=docker`, give `dk` the docker completions with:

```sh
autocomplete alias docker dk   # ~/.config/autocomplete/dk.yaml -> docker's spec
```

Then re-run the `eval` step. `--force` replaces an existing `dk` spec. Since it's a symlink, edits
to the docker spec apply to `dk` too.

`autocomplete alias --list` shows your aliases (`dk -> docker`). To remove one:
`autocomplete alias --rm dk` (TAB after `--rm` lists your aliases). Only
symlinks are removed, never real specs.

See [Writing specs](writing-specs.md) for the full format: all value types, supported YAML
and where specs are looked up.

---

<!-- docs/writing-specs.md -->

# Writing specs

A *spec* is a YAML file that describes one command. Create
`~/.config/autocomplete/<command>.yaml`, then run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again
(or open a new terminal) so bash picks up the new command. Edits to an existing spec take
effect on the next TAB.

## Example

`~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml`:

```yaml
flags:
  -n: {value: {exec: "kubectl get ns -o name | cut -d/ -f2"}, description: Namespace}
  --namespace: {value: {exec: "kubectl get ns -o name | cut -d/ -f2"}, description: Namespace}
  --context: {value: any, description: Name of the kubeconfig context}
  -h: {description: Show help}        # no value
commands:
  get:
    commands:           # fixed words are written as subcommands
      pods: {}
      deployments: {}
      services: {}
  logs:
    flags:
      -f: {description: Stream the logs}
      --tail: {value: any, description: Number of lines to show}
    args:
      exec: kubectl get pods -o name | cut -d/ -f2
  apply:
    flags:
      -f: {value: file, description: File to apply}
  help:
    args: "@subcommands"
```

## Spec format

A spec has these optional keys, and `commands` nests the same structure for subcommands:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `flags` | Map of flag name → flag (see below) |
| `args` | What positional arguments complete to (a value) |
| `commands` | Map of subcommand name → spec |
| `description` | One-line summary shown next to this command when several commands match |
| `aliases` | List of other names for this subcommand, e.g. `aliases: [i, add]` under `install`; each is matched like the main name and shown in its description (`install  -- Install a package (i, add)`); an alias is offered as a candidate only once typed in full |
| `when` | Only list this subcommand if a file in the current directory exists and (optionally) contains a string, e.g. `when: {file: pom.xml, contains: "<artifactId>spotless-maven-plugin</artifactId>"}`. Used for plugin goals that exist only in some projects. A typed command is still recognised either way |
| `examples` | List of `{key, command, description?}` (any level; `key` is a short label, usually the example's flags), shown on TAB after an empty word as `📌 -sS  -- curl -sS https://api.github.com/zen   📚 quiet GET, errors still shown`. Write them yourself (don't copy text from other projects' docs: their licenses may require attribution); meant for commands whose TAB lists nothing else. Hints only: they can't be inserted; when they are the only entries, a `… curl  -- curl: <description>` line (the command name and the spec's `description`, or "type an argument") is added so bash lists them instead of inserting their common prefix |
| `groups` | Map of short-flag letters → `{description?}`, grouping rarely used short flags by meaning. Each key lists the letters of `-x` flags of this spec (or the top-level one) that are hidden from the list and shown together in one entry: `"Up": {description: proxy}` gives `-📌 Up  -- proxy: (U) Proxy user and password (p) HTTP proxy tunnel (using CONNECT)`. Top-level groups apply at every depth. `autocomplete check` reports letters with no matching flag |

Each flag is a map with two optional keys, usually written on one line:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `value` | What the flag's value completes to. Leave it out if the flag takes no value. |
| `description` | One-line summary shown next to the flag when several flags match |
| `show` | `always`: a frequently used flag, never folded into a group or into `-📌` (see below). `collapsed` (short flags only): a rarely used flag, left out of the list and only named in a `📌` entry; still listed when nothing else matches. `default` (or leaving it out): the normal behaviour |

When a short and a long flag with the same description are both listed, only the long one is shown, with the short one as a hint: `--data  -- HTTP POST data (🔥 -d)`. Give a short/long pair the same description to get this.

Flags on the top-level spec are offered after any subcommand too. A flag name ending in `=` (e.g. mvn's `'-Dtest=': {}`) is completed without a trailing space, so you can type the value straight after it; give it a `value` to complete that value too (mvn's `-Dspring-boot.run.profiles=` lists `application-<profile>.*` files). Inside an open quote (`-Dx='-Xmx1g -X`) the last space-separated word is completed, so a quoted value can hold several. Quote such keys in YAML.

On a bare `-<TAB>`, if the command has short flags and 15 or more long ones, only the short ones are listed and the long ones are folded into one last entry, `-📌 --  -- 256 long options: type -- to list`. Type `--<TAB>` to list them.

When the flag list is taller than the terminal, flags are grouped by their next letter: `--content-disposition` and `--content-on-error` fall into one `--c  -- connect-timeout content-disposition content-on-error …` entry. Type `--c<TAB>` (no space is added) to list that group; a big group is split again by the following letter. If all flags in a group share a longer prefix, the entry is that prefix: `--no-  -- no-🧩`. In the name list, names sharing a first word are shown once: `sasl-authzid sasl-ir` → `sasl-🧩`. The smallest groups are then shown in full again while the list still fits, so `node --<TAB>` lists its two `--no-` flags directly.

```yaml
flags:
  --rm: {description: Remove the container when it exits}   # takes no value
  --name: {value: any, description: Assign a name}
  -f: {value: file}
  -q: {}                                                     # no value, no description
```

A value can be:

| Value | Completes to |
|---|---|
| *(empty)*, `~`, `null` | nothing |
| `any` | free text, no suggestions |
| `file` / `dir` | paths / directories only |
| `exec: <shell command>` | one suggestion per output line; `name<TAB>description` shows the description next to it (e.g. `printf '%s\t%s\n' "$pid" "$name"`) |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`suffix: ":"` | appended to each suggestion |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`nospace: true` | don't add a space after accepting it |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`tree: true` | show `a/b` names as `a/` until you type past the `/`, like paths (e.g. `origin/` for remote branches) |
| `"@subcommands"` | the parent command's subcommands (e.g. `git help <TAB>`) |
| `"@command"` | a command from `$PATH`; the words after it are completed with that command's spec (e.g. `sudo`, `xargs`). Words with `=` before the command are skipped (`env FOO=1 git …`). Use it as `args` |
| `"@make-targets"` | targets of the Makefile, with descriptions (see below) |
| `"@make-variables"` | `NAME=` for each upper-case variable (`A-Z`, `0-9`, `_`) the Makefile assigns, for overrides like `make CC=clang` |
| a list `[a, b]` | everything from each item, combined |

Notes:

- Items in a list are value *types*, not literal words: `[pods, deployments]` looks for
  types named `pods` and `deployments`. To offer fixed words, either list them as
  subcommands (`commands: {pods: {}, deployments: {}}`) or use `exec: printf '%s\n' pods deployments`.
- Run `autocomplete check <file>` to validate a spec; errors include line numbers.
- Flags defined at the top level are recognised after any subcommand.
- Descriptions appear when more than one command or flag matches:
  ```
  $ git stash <TAB>
  apply   -- Apply a stash, keeping it
  drop    -- Remove a stash
  pop     -- Apply a stash and remove it
  ...
  ```
  They are plain text: bash 3.2 can't display colors in the completion list. Long
  descriptions are cut to fit the terminal width.
- When one list mixes kinds of suggestions (subcommands, files, make targets and
  variables), each line is tagged, since bash sorts the list and can't show section headers.
  Make variables also show the value the Makefile assigns:
  ```
  $ make D<TAB>
  Dockerfile  -- [target] Generate the Dockerfile
  DESTDIR=    -- [var]    Staging root · ?= /tmp/stage
  ```
  On a bare `make <TAB>` the variables are folded into one display-only `🔧 vars`
  line listing their names, so targets come first. It is never inserted; type a letter
  (`make C<TAB>`) to list matching variables with their values:
  ```
  $ make <TAB>
  all      -- Build everything
  build
  🔧 vars  -- CC PREFIX X
  $ make C<TAB>
  CC=      -- C compiler · ?= cc
  CFLAGS=  -- ?= -O2
  ```
- `"@make-targets"` and `"@make-variables"` read descriptions from the Makefile itself: either `## text` after the
  target or assignment, or the comment lines directly above it (`##` wins if both are present):
  ```make
  # Build the binary
  app: main.c

  test: app  ## Run the test suite
  ```
- `exec` commands run in the current directory, and their errors are discarded.
- Values starting with `@` must be quoted.

## Supported YAML

The YAML reader is built into the binary and covers what specs need: indented mappings and
lists, inline `{...}` and `[...]`, single- and double-quoted strings, and `#` comments.
Anchors, tags and multi-line strings (`|`, `>`) are not supported. Indent with spaces, not
tabs.

A `#` after a space starts a comment, even inside an unquoted value. If a command contains
` #`, quote the whole value:

```yaml
exec: "echo 'not # a comment'"
```

## Where specs are looked up

The first match wins, so your own files override the bundled ones:

1. directories in `$AUTOCOMPLETE_SPECS` (colon-separated)
2. `~/.config/autocomplete`
3. `specs/` next to the binary
4. `../share/autocomplete` relative to the binary (where `make install` puts them)

Files must be named `<command>.yaml` or `<command>.yml`.

The bundled [`specs/`](../specs) (e.g. docker, git, gh, kubectl, make, npm) are good real-world examples.

---

<!-- docs/man-pages.md -->

# Completions from man pages

Most system commands (`ps`, `ls`, `grep`, `tar`, `ssh`, ...) document their options in a
man page. autocomplete can read the page and turn it into flag completion with
descriptions, so you don't have to write a spec by hand.

```sh
autocomplete from man ps ls grep    # writes ~/.config/autocomplete/ps.yaml, ls.yaml, grep.yaml
autocomplete from man --force ps    # overwrite an existing file
```

The result is an ordinary spec. Open it and fix anything the parser got wrong, or add
live values (see [Writing specs](writing-specs.md)). For example, change `-p`'s value in
`ps.yaml` to list running PIDs:

```yaml
  -p:
    value: {exec: "ps -axo pid= | tr -d ' '"}
```

Open a new terminal (or run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again) so the new command is
registered. After a system update changes a man page, run `autocomplete from man --force CMD` to
regenerate the spec (this overwrites your edits).

## What gets extracted

- **Flags**: every option entry in the page, like `-a`, `--text`, or `-A num, --after-context=num`.
- **Descriptions**: the first sentence of each option's text.
- **Values**: a flag takes a value when its entry or the SYNOPSIS shows one (`-O fmt`,
  `[-p pid]`). A value named like a file or path completes files, one named like a
  directory completes directories, and any other value completes nothing.
- **Arguments**: files.

## Limits

- Man pages are free text, so the result is a heuristic. Pages that show example command
  lines at the same indentation as the options (curl, for example) can produce a few extra
  flags.
- Combined short flags like `ls -la` are accepted, but TAB doesn't suggest more letters to
  add to them.
- Values and subcommands are not inferred. Add them by hand to a generated spec.

---

<!-- docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to check |
|---|---|
| Nothing happens on TAB | `complete -p docker` should print `complete -o nospace -C '/path/to/autocomplete _complete' docker`. If not, the `eval` line didn't run; open a new terminal or check your profile. |
| Works in some terminals (e.g. inside `mc`) but not in new Terminal.app windows or tabs | Terminal.app starts login shells, which read `~/.bash_profile` and not `~/.bashrc` (where `make install` puts the `eval` line). Add `[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc` to `~/.bash_profile` instead of copying the `eval` line there. |
| A new spec isn't picked up | Re-run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"`; bash only registers commands at startup. |
| A spec seems to be ignored | `autocomplete check path/to/spec.yaml` shows errors with line numbers. `AUTOCOMPLETE_DEBUG=1` prints errors while completing. |
| No containers / images suggested | The Docker daemon must be running. |
| `source <(autocomplete bash)` does nothing | bash 3.2 bug; use `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"`. |

See also [Cache](cache.md): `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE=1` rules out a stale cache.

---

<!-- docs/how-it-works.md -->

# How it works

`autocomplete bash` prints one `complete -C` line that registers `autocomplete _complete`
for every command that has a spec; no shell function is defined. When you press TAB, bash
runs `autocomplete _complete` with the line and cursor position in `COMP_LINE` and
`COMP_POINT`. The binary splits the line into words and walks the spec. It
then prints the matching suggestions, already escaped for the shell and trimmed the way
bash expects.

bash 3.2 lacks `compopt` and `mapfile`, so nothing here relies on them. Commands are
registered with `complete -o nospace`, and the binary adds the trailing space itself to
finished words.

Descriptions use the way bash handles several matches: it inserts only their common
prefix and lists the rest. When more than one command matches, the binary returns each
one as `name  -- description`, padded so bash lists one per line. The names differ before
the padding starts, so the descriptions are only displayed, never typed into the command
line. A single match is returned as the bare name. bash 3.2 shows escape codes literally
(`^[[2m`), so the list can't use color.

---

<!-- docs/cache.md -->

# Cache

Specs larger than 100 KB are compiled to `~/.cache/autocomplete/<command>.cache`
(`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/autocomplete` if set). Smaller specs are read straight from the YAML on
every TAB; at that size the cache saves nothing (see below). A cache file is used only while
it's newer than its YAML and was built from the same file; otherwise it's rebuilt
automatically on the next TAB.

- `autocomplete cache` (or `make cache`) rebuilds the cache for every big spec now.
- `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE=1` turns the cache off.
- `rm -rf ~/.cache/autocomplete` resets it.

## When it matters

For specs of normal size the cache makes no noticeable difference. Measured on a MacBook,
a TAB takes about 5 ms with or without the cache for all bundled specs (docker, git, make,
each under 10 KB). That time is mostly starting the program, and an `exec` command such as
`docker ps` usually takes far longer than that.

The cache starts to pay off only for very large specs, hence the 100 KB threshold:

| Spec size | With cache | Without cache |
|---|---|---|
| ~20 KB | ~5 ms | ~5 ms |
| ~200 KB | ~7 ms | ~9 ms |
| ~1 MB | ~17 ms | ~28 ms |

So turning it off with `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE=1` is safe if it ever gets in the way.
